lesson.title: Genetic Recombination: Assembling New Combinations of Alleles
lesson.summary: Genetic recombination is the production of chromosomes carrying new combinations of alleles, most directly through crossing over at chiasmata during meiosis, and it is one of the main reasons offspring are not exact genetic copies of either parent.
lesson.body:
Genetic recombination refers to any outcome in which a chromosome passed to a gamete carries a combination of alleles that did not exist together on either of the original chromosomes an individual inherited from their own parents. In meiosis, the main way this happens is crossing over, the reciprocal exchange of DNA between non-sister chromatids that takes place at chiasmata, as described in the previous two chapters. It is worth being precise about this, because recombination is often confused with a different process, independent assortment of whole chromosomes, which will come up as its own topic soon. The distinction matters: independent assortment shuffles which whole chromosome, maternal or paternal, ends up in a gamete, while recombination through crossing over shuffles alleles within a single chromosome, breaking up combinations that were previously locked together on the same piece of DNA.

Why does this matter biologically? Genetic variation is the raw material that natural selection acts on, and recombination is a major contributor to it. Because of recombination, full siblings who inherit chromosomes from the very same two parents still end up with different specific combinations of alleles, since the chromosomes that get passed down are not simply intact copies of a parent's original chromosomes but often mosaics reshuffled by crossing over. Combined with independent assortment, this means that, aside from identical twins, essentially every gamete a person produces carries a genetically unique set of chromosomes.

Returning to the two-gene example from the crossing over chapter helps make this concrete. If a chromosome carries alleles A and B together, and its homolog carries a and b together, gametes without any crossover between those two loci carry the parental combinations AB or ab. Gametes that result from a crossover between the two loci carry the recombinant combinations Ab or aB, combinations that are new relative to either parental chromosome. Geneticists can actually use the frequency of these recombinant offspring, compared to parental-type offspring, to estimate how physically close two genes are on a chromosome. Genes that sit very close together are less likely to have a crossover happen between them, so they show a low recombination frequency and tend to be inherited together, while genes farther apart on the same chromosome recombine more often.

In short, recombination through crossing over at chiasmata is one of meiosis's two great variation-generating tools, working alongside independent assortment to ensure that the gametes an organism produces are not just a reduced copy of its own chromosomes, but genuinely new combinations, ready to be passed on to the next generation.
